A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe WeatherDiffusion, and all supplied pages, equations, figures and tables are readable. However, neither includes the repeatedly referenced supplementary material. Training details and some additional analyses therefore cannot be compared, including v2's detailed distillation, progressive-training and user-study procedures.

before.justification: v1 reports original inverse-rendering measurements and an attention ablation in Table 2, alongside forward-rendering and downstream perception examples in Figures 9–12.

after.justification: v2 reports original rendering and editing measurements, ACDC detection and segmentation results, ablations, and a 61-participant user study.

M1.justification: v1's MAA constructs visual conditioning through map-token attention and semantic embeddings. v2's IMAA instead constructs an MLP-based mask that biases DiT joint attention. v2 also introduces CLIP-space weather interpolation, feature distillation from the original diffusion model, and heuristic-guided progressive attention training. These change the procedure beyond renaming.

E1.justification: v2 adds graded rain/snow editing scenarios, ACDC evaluation, human preference assessment and a video-sequence test of temporal consistency. These broaden evaluation beyond v1's discrete still-image rendering and qualitative perception examples. The underlying driving-scene domain remains, while nighttime coverage is no longer listed for WeatherSynthetic.

E2.justification: v2 retains the earlier inverse-rendering table comparators and adds DiffusionRenderer, previously only cited. It also evaluates Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, WeatherWeaver and Instruct-Pix2Pix in editing comparisons, and AWRaCLe and Histoformer in qualitative restoration/perception comparisons. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Reported dataset sizes change from 35K/10K to 38K/18K for WeatherSynthetic/WeatherReal. WeatherReal changes from a stated evaluation dataset to explicitly training-only. New protocols include PickScore, CLIP-S and DINO-S editing evaluation, ACDC validation metrics, and voting by 61 participants on eight cases. These are substantive setting and evaluation-design changes.

E4.justification: v2 revises the attention ablation for IMAA and adds a forward-renderer WeatherReal ablation, weather-intensity comparisons and a temporal-consistency case study. v1 instead describes dataset ablations for inverse rendering and displays a dense-fog failure case. The handrail attention example is partly retained, rather than entirely new evidence.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's participant count and average preference describe a new study and its result, without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Reported proposed-method albedo PSNR changes from 18.02 in v1 Table 2 to 27.99 in v2 Table 3; normal PSNR changes from 20.95 to 25.06. Method and data revisions prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains. v2 also adds editing scores, ACDC results including AP75 13.15→24.60 and mIoU 24.13→30.05, and 81.67% user preference.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for CLIP weather directions and interpolation, and replaces the map-conditioning formulas with MLP-mask and attention-bias definitions. These are local mathematical specifications accompanying the method changes. Neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the assumption linking weather effects primarily to irradiance remains.

C1.justification: v2 makes fine-grained intrinsic-space weather editing and advantages over pixel-space editing/restoration central claims, extending v1's general forward/inverse-rendering framing. CLIP-based continuous control becomes a prominent contribution. Intrinsic decomposition, map-aware guidance and the two datasets remain shared contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's discussion of unseen objects and dense-fog sky/building errors with a temporal-consistency limitation and video-model resource tradeoffs. It also adds substantive interpretations of geometry preservation, surface-weather removal and lighting, and explains why higher PickScore or DINO similarity need not indicate more successful weather editing.

D1.justification: v2 revises the data-construction description from InstructPix2Pix plus depth/noise-based augmentation to Flux-Kontext, and adds multimodal filtering and manual pseudo-label checks. It newly promises dataset release upon acceptance, without providing released resources. Rendering tools and approximately 24-hour generation time remain; important training details still depend on unavailable supplementary material.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a broad generative/inverse-rendering survey toward positioning against pixel-space editing, intrinsic-space object editing and 3D weather editing. Substantive additions include WeatherWeaver, IntrinsicEdit, Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image, ClimateNeRF, WeatherEdit and UniRelight, supporting a substantially revised novelty argument.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around controllable weather editing. The separate background section disappears, dataset construction moves into Method, and experiments are reorganized around editing/restoration comparisons before rendering components. The former Applications discussion is integrated into downstream evaluation.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the teaser and pipeline diagrams, adds editing and ACDC tables, and introduces multi-method editing grids, intensity comparisons, dataset-ablation panels and a video example. The dataset-comparison table disappears. Some earlier rendering and attention panels are retained, cropped or relocated within a substantially redesigned layout.

improvement.justification: v1 supported weather-editing and downstream-benefit claims mainly through examples; v2 makes them more assessable through relevant comparators, quantitative evaluations and a reported user study. The gain is limited by unavailable procedural details and omitted earlier failure discussion. Reporting problems also remain: the all-metrics claim conflicts with Table 3's albedo LPIPS, and Table 2's detection mAP values are inconsistent with its AP50/AP75 values under standard averaging.
